title: Checkpoint: Making Sense of Numbers
objective: After this level you can explain what percentages, percentage points, rates and big numbers really say, and spot when one is misused.
summary: Every share hides an "out of what": 100 for a percent, the start for a percent change, the population for a rate, N for "1 in N". Ask it, and check scale and precision too.

cards.headline: "Up 50%!" Before you're impressed, ask: 50% of what?
cards.body: Chapter 1 has handed you a toolkit for everyday numbers. This checkpoint puts it to work on the question hiding behind every one of them.

cards.headline: Every share hides an "out of what"
cards.body: A percent is out of 100. A percent change is out of the starting value. A rate is out of the population. "1 in N" is out of N. Each one compares a part with a whole, so the first question for any of them is the same: out of what? Change the whole and the same part tells a different story.

items.label: Totals vs. rates
points: Divide by the population to compare

cards.headline: Big and precise aren't the same as right
cards.body: Two last checks. Scale: a billion is a thousand millions, so picture it in seconds (almost 32 years) before you nod along. Precision: 98.6°F looked exact, yet it came from a round 37°C. A number is only as sharp as the measuring behind it.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: How to turn any share into a percent, and why to ask of every number: out of what?
Why a 50% fall followed by a 50% rise leaves you below where you started.
What separates percentage points from percent, and totals from rates per person.
How big a billion really is, and why 98.6°F looks more precise than it is.

questions.prompt: For a rate per 100,000 people, what is the "out of what"?

options.label: The starting value
options.rationale: That's the whole for a percent change.

options.label: The number of cases
options.rationale: Cases are the part, not the whole.
That's the whole for a percent.

questions.explanation: A rate divides the count (the part) by the population (the whole).

questions.prompt: A price rises 50%, then falls 50%. Compared with where it started, the price is:

options.label: Back where it began
options.rationale: The fall is taken from the higher price, so it removes more.

options.label: 25% higher
options.rationale: Equal percent moves up and down always end below the start.

questions.explanation: $100 up 50% is $150; down 50% from $150 is $75, which is 25% below the start.

questions.prompt: A school's pass rate goes from 40% to 50%. Which statement is correct?

options.label: It rose 10 percent, from 40% to 50%
options.rationale: The 10 is percentage points; as a percent change it is 10 ÷ 40, or 25%.

options.label: It rose 25 percentage points
options.rationale: 25 is the percent increase, not the points.

questions.explanation: Subtract for points (50 minus 40 = 10 points); divide by the start for percent (10 ÷ 40 = 25%).

questions.prompt: Town A has 20 cases among 1,000 people. City B has 200 cases among 100,000 people. Which has the higher rate?

options.label: City B, because it has more cases
options.rationale: More cases, but spread over far more people.

options.label: Town A, ten times higher than City B
You can't tell without percents
options.rationale: Dividing each count by its population is enough.

questions.explanation: Town A: 20 ÷ 1,000 is 2,000 per 100,000. City B: 200 per 100,000. Town A's rate is ten times higher.

questions.prompt: What does the story of 98.6°F teach about any number you read?

options.label: Fahrenheit is less accurate than Celsius
options.rationale: Neither scale is the problem; the conversion added digits.

options.label: Round numbers are always wrong
options.rationale: 37°C was a fair round figure; it just wasn't as sharp as 98.6 looks.

options.label: It can look more exact than its measurement
Old studies should be ignored
options.rationale: Wunderlich's study was huge; the lesson is about precision.

questions.explanation: A number is only as sharp as its measurement. Converting a round 37°C gave 98.6, a decimal from a formula.
